title: Kansas City Smoked Brisket
seoTitle: Kansas City Smoked Brisket | Firefighter Meal
shortDescription: Low-and-slow smoke for the whole crew
subtitle: Low-and-slow smoke for the whole crew
description: Low-and-slow smoke for the whole crew. Sized for a full crew, with timing that still works when the kitchen gets interrupted.

ingredients.name: Whole packer brisket, trimmed
ingredients.notes: about 12 oz raw per firefighter after trim

steps.title: Trim and season
steps.instruction: Trim hard fat cap to ¼ inch. Score the fat cap lightly. Slather with mustard if using, then coat heavily with salt and pepper (Texas-style is salt and pepper only — that's fine). Rest seasoned brisket 1 hour at room temp while the smoker comes up.

steps.title: Smoke until bark sets
steps.instruction: Run smoker at 250–275°F with oak or hickory. Place brisket fat-cap up. Smoke unwrapped until bark is dark mahogany and internal temp hits 165–170°F in the flat (roughly 6–8 hours). Spritz with vinegar and broth every 90 minutes if the surface looks dry.

steps.title: Wrap the stall
steps.instruction: When the flat stalls around 165°F or bark is set, wrap tightly in butcher paper or foil with a splash of broth. Return to smoker until probe slides like butter into the flat at 203–205°F (another 3–5 hours).

steps.title: Rest and slice
steps.instruction: Rest wrapped brisket in a cooler or warm oven (170°F) at least 1 hour — up to 3 for a hall feed. Slice against the grain: flat in thin slices, point chopped for burnt-end style bites. Hold slices in broth-lined pans covered with foil at 180°F for late eaters.

proTips: Keep a backup tray warm in the oven for late calls — nothing worse than cold plates after a run.
Taste for salt at the end — hall palates run salty after long shifts.
Rest grilled proteins 5–8 minutes under foil before slicing — juices stay in the meat.
tonightSpread: Plate Kansas City Smoked Brisket with sides in separate pans so the crew can mix portions.
Line up Kansas City Smoked Brisket on the main counter with serving spoons — firefighters grab fast between calls.
Keep a backup tray warm in the oven at 200°F for late arrivals after a run.
Slice proteins on a cutting board at the end of the line so everyone sees the smoke ring and char.
Set sauce and pickles on the side — sauced meat holds better on the backup tray.
leftovers: Cool leftovers in shallow containers within two hours — deep pots stay hot too long.
Label trays with date and reheat to 165°F minimum before second shift.
Slice cold protein thin for next-day wraps or salads — faster reheat, less dry-out.
whyCrewsLikeIt: Low-and-slow smoke for the whole crew. A hall pick for regular dinner nights — one line, real portions, no drama at the stove.
